t: Check the reticulocyte count before treating this as a megaloblastic picture. Reticulocytes are larger than mature red cells, so a brisk reticulocytosis raises the MCV by itself — if the reticulocytes are up, the macrocytosis may be a consequence of a responding marrow rather than of B12 or folate deficiency, and the question becomes where the blood is being lost or destroyed.

The HbA2 is above the range beta-thalassaemia trait produces. A result this high is not an A2 fraction: a haemoglobin variant is almost certainly co-eluting in the A2 window on the HPLC trace. Confirmatory: ask the laboratory to review the chromatogram and identify the variant - haemoglobin E is the commonest cause of this pattern in South and South-East Asia, and HbE trait, HbE/beta-thalassaemia and HbE disease carry very different implications from each other. Management suggestion: do not report or counsel this as beta-thalassaemia trait; the variant needs to be named first. Verify all doses per formulary.

t: The HbA2 is 4.0 per cent or more, but the red-cell indices are not both reduced. The Indian national guideline (NHM 2016, Table 4) diagnoses beta-thalassaemia trait at HbA2 4.0-8.0 per cent only with a reduced MCV and MCH, so this is not recorded as trait. BSH 2023 advises that an HbA2 above 4 per cent with a normal MCH should be assessed further: it may indicate a milder beta-thalassaemia carrier state, or accompany alpha-thalassaemia or vitamin B12 or folate deficiency. In pregnancy BSH 2023 advises that it warrants testing the baby's biological father.

t: Where a haptoglobin has been measured, interpret it with its confounders in mind. It is an acute-phase reactant, so inflammation, smoking or nephrotic syndrome can raise it into the normal range and mask genuine haemolysis; and it is low without haemolysis in liver impairment, malnutrition and congenital haptoglobin deficiency. A raised LDH is likewise not specific — it also rises in myocardial infarction, hepatitis, tumours, and in B12 or folate deficiency, where it reflects ineffective erythropoiesis rather than red-cell destruction.

The HbA2 is above the range beta-thalassaemia trait produces. A result this high is not an A2 fraction: a haemoglobin variant is almost certainly co-eluting in the A2 window on the HPLC trace. Confirmatory: ask the laboratory to review the chromatogram and identify the variant - haemoglobin E is the commonest cause of this pattern in South and South-East Asia, and HbE trait, HbE/beta-thalassaemia and HbE disease carry very different implications from each other. Management suggestion: do not report or counsel this as beta-thalassaemia trait; the variant needs to be named first. Verify all doses per formulary.

t: The HbA2 is above the range beta-thalassaemia trait produces. A result this high is not an A2 fraction: a haemoglobin variant is almost certainly co-eluting in the A2 window on the HPLC trace. Confirmatory: ask the laboratory to review the chromatogram and identify the variant - haemoglobin E is the commonest cause of this pattern in South and South-East Asia, and HbE trait, HbE/beta-thalassaemia and HbE disease carry very different implications from each other. Management suggestion: do not report or counsel this as beta-thalassaemia trait; the variant needs to be named first. Verify all doses per formulary.

The HbA2 is 4.0 per cent or more, but the red-cell indices are not both reduced. The Indian national guideline (NHM 2016, Table 4) diagnoses beta-thalassaemia trait at HbA2 4.0-8.0 per cent only with a reduced MCV and MCH, so this is not recorded as trait. BSH 2023 advises that an HbA2 above 4 per cent with a normal MCH should be assessed further: it may indicate a milder beta-thalassaemia carrier state, or accompany alpha-thalassaemia or vitamin B12 or folate deficiency. In pregnancy BSH 2023 advises that it warrants testing the baby's biological father.

The Indian national guideline (NHM 2016, Table 4) diagnoses beta-thalassaemia trait at HbA2 4.0-8.0 per cent only with a reduced MCV and MCH, so this is not recorded as trait. BSH 2023 advises that an HbA2 above 4 per cent with a normal MCH should be assessed further: it may indicate a milder beta-thalassaemia carrier state, or accompany alpha-thalassaemia or vitamin B12 or folate deficiency. In pregnancy BSH 2023 advises that it warrants testing the baby's biological father.

t: The absolute eosinophil count is at or above 1.5 x10^9/L. At this level a cause should be sought irrespective of whether organ damage is suspected, which is what separates this from a mild eosinophilia that may need no further testing. Confirmatory: repeat the count to establish whether it is persistent, and work through the causes - stool ova and parasites for helminths, and in endemic areas consider filariasis or tropical pulmonary eosinophilia; a drug reaction; atopy or asthma; and, where no reactive cause emerges or the count persists, a clonal cause needing haematology review. SAFETY - before any corticosteroid is given, cover for Strongyloides with ivermectin or exclude infection: steroids can precipitate hyperinfection syndrome, which carries very high mortality, exposure may be decades old, and a negative travel history does not exclude it. Management suggestion: treat the cause once identified; if a drug is implicated, review and stop the culprit with the clinician. Verify all doses per formulary.

There is anaemia with small red cells. The morphology is established; the cause is not, because the results that separate the causes were not supplied. In this setting the two that matter most are iron deficiency and thalassaemia trait, and they are managed very differently - iron given to a trait carrier does not help and iron withheld from a deficient patient leaves a treatable anaemia untreated. Confirmatory: a ferritin separates them in most cases, read alongside a CRP because ferritin rises with inflammation and a normal value does not exclude deficiency when inflammation is present. Where the ferritin is normal or the indices still conflict, haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC for HbA2 types the trait. The red cell count and the RDW already on this report point one way or the other but do not settle it. Management suggestion: do not start iron on the morphology alone; the ferritin usually returns quickly enough to start on a result rather than a guess. Verify all doses per formulary.

The red cells are small. The Mentzer index sits between 12 and 14, where it cannot separate iron deficiency from thalassaemia trait, and no confirmatory result has been supplied. A second index, the Patra index (MCV divided by RDW-CV), reads below its 5.3 cut-point, which leans towards iron deficiency. Read that as a lean and nothing more: it comes from a single-centre study of 406 people aged 3 to 50, so it is not an adult series. Confirmatory: a ferritin with a CRP is the cheapest and most decisive next step, and it settles this without relying on the index at all. Where iron is replete, HbA2 types the trait instead. Management suggestion: a lean is not a reason to start iron before the ferritin is back, and iron deficiency in an adult raises the separate question of where the iron is being lost. Verify all doses per formulary.

In this setting the two that matter most are iron deficiency and thalassaemia trait, and they are managed very differently - iron given to a trait carrier does not help and iron withheld from a deficient patient leaves a treatable anaemia untreated. The HbA2 falls in the equivocal band, between the normal range and the level that supports beta-thalassaemia trait. This is NOT a diagnosis of trait and should not be recorded as one: the national guideline requires detailed evaluation before trait is concluded from this band. The commonest reason a genuine carrier sits here is co-existing iron deficiency, which lowers HbA2 and can mask the trait. Confirmatory: check iron status, correct any deficiency, and REPEAT the HbA2 after repletion - the repeat is what settles it. If iron is replete and the HbA2 remains in this band, the laboratory should be asked about the alpha-globin genotype, since alpha-thalassaemia trait runs a normal or low HbA2 and cannot be excluded by this result. Management suggestion: do not begin family or antenatal counselling on this result alone. Verify all doses per formulary.

The HbA2 falls in the equivocal band, between the normal range and the level that supports beta-thalassaemia trait. This is NOT a diagnosis of trait and should not be recorded as one: the national guideline requires detailed evaluation before trait is concluded from this band. The commonest reason a genuine carrier sits here is co-existing iron deficiency, which lowers HbA2 and can mask the trait. If iron is replete and the HbA2 remains in this band, the laboratory should be asked about the alpha-globin genotype, since alpha-thalassaemia trait runs a normal or low HbA2 and cannot be excluded by this result. Management suggestion: do not begin family or antenatal counselling on this result alone. Verify all doses per formulary.

There is anaemia with small red cells. The morphology is established; the cause is not, because the results that separate the causes were not supplied. In this setting the two that matter most are iron deficiency and thalassaemia trait, and they are managed very differently - iron given to a trait carrier does not help and iron withheld from a deficient patient leaves a treatable anaemia untreated. Confirmatory: a ferritin separates them in most cases, read alongside a CRP because ferritin rises with inflammation and a normal value does not exclude deficiency when inflammation is present. Where the ferritin is normal or the indices still conflict, haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC for HbA2 types the trait. The red cell count and the RDW already on this report point one way or the other but do not settle it. Management suggestion: do not start iron on the morphology alone; the ferritin usually returns quickly enough to start on a result rather than a guess. Verify all doses per formulary.

There is anaemia with small red cells. The morphology is established; the cause is not, because the results that separate the causes were not supplied. In this setting the two that matter most are iron deficiency and thalassaemia trait, and they are managed very differently - iron given to a trait carrier does not help and iron withheld from a deficient patient leaves a treatable anaemia untreated. Confirmatory: a ferritin separates them in most cases, read alongside a CRP because ferritin rises with inflammation and a normal value does not exclude deficiency when inflammation is present. Where the ferritin is normal or the indices still conflict, haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC for HbA2 types the trait. The red cell count and the RDW already on this report point one way or the other but do not settle it. Management suggestion: do not start iron on the morphology alone; the ferritin usually returns quickly enough to start on a result rather than a guess. Verify all doses per formulary.
